seoTitle: How to Set Up International Shipping on eBay to Sell Global
metaDescription: Enable international shipping on eBay by choosing between International Standard Delivery, the Global Shipping Program, and custom shipping rates.
intro: International shipping on eBay isn't a separate account you sign up for — it's a toggle sitting right inside each listing's shipping section, next to the domestic options you're probably already used to setting. That makes it easy to overlook, but also easy to turn on once you know where it lives. This guide walks through enabling it on an actual listing: picking a domestic service first, flipping on the international switch, choosing which countries you'll ship to, and understanding why the price jumps once a package is headed overseas.

steps.heading: Open the listing you want to ship internationally
steps.body: International shipping is set per listing, so start from an item you've already listed or are in the process of listing — here, a used copy of Atomic Habits. From your Selling area, find the item and open it for editing rather than trying to hunt for a global shipping switch somewhere in account settings, because there isn't one; every listing carries its own shipping configuration.

image.caption: A single item listing open for editing — this is where shipping options, domestic and international, actually get configured.

steps.heading: Set your domestic shipping service first
steps.body: Before touching international options, the Shipping service section asks you to pick a domestic carrier and service level — USPS Media Mail, UPS Ground Saver, or USPS Ground Advantage, each with its own delivery window, price, and compensation coverage if something goes wrong in transit. eBay marks one option "Recommended" and shows buying a label through eBay as the way to unlock the discounted rate buyers see on your listing. The "Who pays?" toggle just below lets you decide whether the buyer covers this cost or you build it into the item price.

image.caption: The domestic Shipping service picker, with USPS and UPS options compared side by side and a Buyer pays / Seller pays toggle underneath.

steps.heading: Turn on the International shipping toggle
steps.body: Scroll past the domestic section and you'll find International shipping as its own block with a switch on the right — off by default on most listings. Flipping it on reveals a Destination field and a separate shipping service picker specific to cross-border delivery. This is the actual mechanism the video title refers to: there's no dedicated "go global" wizard, just this toggle inside the listing you're already editing.

image.caption: International shipping switched on, with Destination set to Worldwide and USPS First Class Package International selected as the carrier service.

steps.heading: Choose how wide your destination reach goes
steps.body: The Destination dropdown defaults to Worldwide once international shipping is on, which is the simplest setting if you're comfortable shipping to any country that can legally receive the item. If you'd rather limit exposure to certain regions — because of customs complexity, high loss rates, or items with export restrictions — this is also where you'd narrow that list instead of leaving it wide open. Start broad and dial it back once you see which countries actually convert, rather than guessing upfront which ones to exclude.

steps.heading: Pick an international shipping service level
steps.body: With Worldwide selected, eBay surfaced USPS First Class Package International as the service, listing up to $100 in compensation, a 4 lb / 24 inch size limit, and a price range rather than a flat number — in this case a buyer cost spanning from the mid-$20s to the low-$40s. That range reflects the fact that international rates vary by destination country even under one service tier, which is why eBay shows a band instead of a single price the way domestic listings do.

steps.heading: Decide who pays for the international leg
steps.body: Just like the domestic section, international shipping has its own buyer-pays or seller-pays choice. Because cross-border rates run noticeably higher than domestic ones, many sellers pass this cost directly to the buyer rather than baking an unpredictable range into every price, especially when Worldwide is selected and the true cost depends entirely on where the buyer is located.

steps.heading: Expect a bigger jump than the timestamps suggest
steps.body: It's worth comparing the numbers side by side: the same package that ships domestically for under five dollars jumps to a price range in the tens of dollars once it's headed abroad. That's not a mistake in the settings — it's the real cost difference between a domestic parcel and international package handling, customs paperwork, and longer-distance carriage. Set buyer expectations for that gap in your listing description so a shopper in another country isn't caught off guard at checkout.

faq.question: What's the difference between Global Shipping Program and Standard Delivery?
faq.answer: Global Shipping Program handles international logistics on eBay's end, while International Standard Delivery and custom rates give sellers more direct control over shipping.

faq.question: Can I exclude certain countries from international shipping?
faq.answer: Yes — once international shipping is turned on for a listing, the Destination field can be narrowed from Worldwide to specific regions or countries instead.

faq.question: What causes delays or cancellations with international orders?
faq.answer: Missing or inaccurate customs information and delivery estimates are common causes of shipping delays and order cancellations.

faq.question: Is international shipping complicated to set up on eBay?
faq.answer: Not really — it's a single toggle inside each listing's shipping section, right below the domestic shipping service you're already choosing.

faq.question: Why is the international shipping price shown as a range instead of one number?
faq.answer: When the destination is set to Worldwide, actual rates vary by country, so eBay displays a price band that reflects the cheapest and most expensive destinations covered by that service.
